'''Aaron Robertson''' (born November 8, 1971) is an American [[mathematician]] who specializes in [[Ramsey theory]]. He is a [[professor]] at [[Colgate University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Aaron Robertson {{!}} Colgate University|url=https://www.colgate.edu/about/directory/arobertson|access-date=2021-10-17|website=www.colgate.edu|language=en}}</ref>

== Life and education ==
Aaron Robertson was born in [[Torrance, California]], and moved with his parents to [[Midland, Michigan]] at the age of 4. He studied [[actuarial science]] as an [[Undergraduate education|undergraduate]] at the [[University of Michigan]], and went on to graduate school in [[mathematics]] at [[Temple University]] in [[Philadelphia]], where he was supervised by [[Doron Zeilberger]]. Robertson received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1999 with his thesis titled ''Some New Results in Ramsey Theory''.<ref name=":0"/>

Following his Ph.D., Robertson became an [[assistant professor]] of mathematics at [[Colgate University]], where he is currently a full professor.

== Mathematical work ==
Robertson's work in mathematics since 1998 has consisted predominantly of topics related to [[Ramsey theory]].

One of Robertson's earliest publications is a paper, co-authored with his supervisor Doron Zeilberger, which came out of his Ph.D. work. The authors prove that "the minimum number (asymptotically) of monochromatic [[Schur's theorem|Schur Triples]] that a 2-colouring of <math>[1,n]</math> can have <math display="inline">n^2/22 + O(n)</math>".<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Robertson|first1=Aaron|last2=Zeilberger|first2=Doron|date=1998-03-25|title=A 2-Coloring of $[1,N]$ can have $(1/22)N^2+O(N)$ Monochromatic Schur Triples, but not less!|url=https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v5i1r19|journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics|volume=5 |language=en|pages=R19|doi=10.37236/1357|issn=1077-8926|doi-access=free}}</ref> 

After completing his dissertation, Robertson worked with 3-term [[Arithmetic progression|arithmetic progressions]] where he found the best-known values that were close to each other and titled this piece ''New Lower Bounds for Some Multicolored Ramsey Numbers''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Robertson|first=Aaron|date=1999|title=New Lower Bounds for Some Multicolored Ramsey Numbers|url=https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v6i1r3|journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics|volume=6 |language=en|pages=R3|doi=10.37236/1435|issn=1077-8926|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Another notable piece of Robertson's research is a paper co-authored with Doron Zeilberger and [[Herbert Wilf]] titled ''Permutation Patterns and Continued Fractions''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Robertson|first1=Aaron|last2=Wilf|first2=Herbert S.|last3=Zeilberger|first3=Doron|date=1999-10-01|title=Permutation Patterns and Continued Fractions|url=https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v6i1r38|journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics|volume=6 |language=en|pages=R38|doi=10.37236/1470|issn=1077-8926|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In the paper, they "find a generating function for the number of (132)-avoiding permutations that have a given number of (123) patterns"<ref name=":1" /> with the result being "in the form of a continued fraction".<ref name=":1" /> Robertson's contribution to this specific paper includes discussion on permutations that avoid a certain pattern but contain others.

A notable paper Robertson wrote titled ''A Probalistic Threshold For Monochromatic Arithmetic Progressions''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Robertson|first=Aaron|date=2016-01-01|title=A probabilistic threshold for monochromatic arithmetic progressions|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series A|language=en|volume=137|pages=79–87|doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2015.08.003|doi-access=free|issn=0097-3165|arxiv=1206.2885}}</ref> explores the function <math>f_r(k) = \sqrt k \cdot r^{k/2}</math> (where <math>r\geq 2</math> is fixed) and the r-colourings of <math>[1,n_k] = \{1,2,\ldots,n_k\}</math>. Robertson analyzes the threshold function for <math>k</math>-term arithmetic progressions and improves the bounds found previously.

In 2004, Robertson and Bruce M. Landman published the book ''Ramsey Theory on the Integers'', of which a second expanded edition appeared in 2014.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Landman|first1=Bruce M.|last2=Robertson|first2=Aaron|url=http://www.ams.org/books/stml/073/|title=Ramsey Theory on the Integers|edition=2nd|volume=73|date=2014|publisher=The Student Mathematical Library|isbn=978-1-4704-2000-0|doi=10.1090/stml/073}}</ref> The book introduced new topics such as rainbow Ramsey theory, an “inequality” version of [[Schur's theorem]], monochromatic solutions of [[Recurrence relation|recurrence relations]], Ramsey results involving both sums and products, monochromatic sets avoiding certain differences, Ramsey properties for polynomial progressions, generalizations of the '''Erdős–Ginzberg–Ziv''' theorem, and the number of [[Arithmetic progression|arithmetic progressions]] under arbitrary colourings.

More recently, in 2021, Robertson published a book titled ''Fundamentals of Ramsey Theory.''<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Robertson|first=Aaron|url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/9780429431418/fundamentals-ramsey-theory-aaron-robertson|title=Fundamentals of Ramsey Theory|date=2021-06-18|publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC|isbn=978-0-429-43141-8|location=Boca Raton|doi=10.1201/9780429431418|s2cid=234866085 }}</ref> Robertson's goal in writing this book was to "help give an overview of Ramsey theory from several points of view, adding intuition and detailed proofs as we go, while being, hopefully, a bit gentler than most of the other books on Ramsey theory".<ref name=":3" /> Throughout the book, Robertson discusses several theorems including [[Ramsey's theorem|Ramsey's Theorem]], [[Van der Waerden's theorem|Van der Waerden's Theorem]], [[Rado's theorem (Ramsey theory)|Rado's Theorem]], and [[Hales–Jewett theorem|Hales–Jewett Theorem]].
